Ashish Sharma vs Collector Shajapur on 5 February, 2026
 Neutral Citation No. 2025:Mphc-Ind:33970
 1 Neutral Citation No. 2026:Mphc-Ind:4156
 1 W.P. No. 28731/2024
 W.P. No.43709/2025
 In The High Court Of Madhya Pradesh

At Indore
 Before
 Hon'Ble Shri Justice Jai Kumar Pillai
 On The 5th Of February, 2026
 Writ Petition No. 28731 of 2024
 Ashish Sharma
 Versus
 Collector Shajapur And Others
 Appearance:
 Shri Manish Yadav - Advocate for the petitioner.
 Shri Pradyumna Kibe - Ga for the respondents/State.
 Order

By this petition filed under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, the petitioner invokes the extraordinary jurisdiction of this Court, challenging the legality, validity, and propriety of the order dated 20.03.2012 (Annexure P/3) passed by Respondent No. 3, whereby the 2 NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-IND:4156 services of the petitioner were terminated.
The petitioner further challenges the order dated 17.09.2024 (Annexure P/18), whereby the representation of the petitioner seeking reinstatement was rejected by the respondents.

The petitioner prays for the issuance of a writ in the nature of Certiorari to quash the impugned orders and a writ of Mandamus directing the respondents to reinstate the petitioner in service with all consequential benefits,
including back wages.
2. The facts, as strictly discernible from the record, are that the petitioner was initially appointed to the post of Samvida Shala Shikshak Varg-2 on 18.08.2001.
Subsequently, by an order dated 30.06.2008, the petitioner was absorbed/appointed as a permanent teacher.

It is the case of the petitioner that an F.I.R. bearing Crime No. 902/2011 was registered against him at Police Station Kotwali, District Shajapur, for offences punishable under Sections 420, 467, 468, 471, and 34 of the Indian Penal Code.

The allegation levelled was that the brother of the petitioner had issued a false Ashish Sharma vs Collector Shajapur on 5 February, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/188793031/
1 teaching experience certificate, which the petitioner utilized to secure his appointment.
3. Pursuant to the registration of the said F.I.R., the Respondent No. 3, vide order dated 20.03.2012,
dismissed the petitioner from service.
The petitioner contends that this dismissal was effected without affording him any proper opportunity of hearing.
Aggrieved by the 3 NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-IND:4156 termination, the petitioner submitted a representation on 11.07.2012 to the respondents, asserting that the dismissal was unconstitutional.
Further representations were made to the Commissioner, Ujjain, on 18.07.2012, and a legal notice was issued on 23.10.2012.

Despite correspondence between the Commissioner, Ujjain, and the CEO (Respondents) regarding the pending representation, and a reply from the Commissioner dated 11.08.2014 stating that the matter was sub- judice, the petitioner remained out of service.
4. The criminal trial concluded with the judgment dated 28.03.2023 passed in S.T. No.73/2015.
The learned Trial Court acquitted the petitioner of all charges.
Crucially, the learned Trial Court opined that the certificate in question was not forged.
Following the acquittal, the petitioner submitted representations dated 24.04.2023, 07.07.2023, and 31.07.2023 seeking reinstatement.
When no action was taken, the petitioner approached this Court in W.P. No. 896/2024.
This Court, vide order dated 11.07.2024, directed the respondents to decide the petitioner's representation.

In compliance thereof, the Respondent No. 3 passed the impugned order dated 17.09.2024, rejecting the representation on the premise that a Criminal Appeal (No. 10847/2023) preferred by the State against the acquittal is pending.

5. Learned counsel for the petitioner submits that the impugned 4 NEUTRAL CITATION NO.
2026:MPHC-IND:4156 order dated 17.09.2024 is illegal, perverse, and liable to be set aside.
It is contended that the petitioner, having been honourably acquitted by the learned Trial Court, is entitled to reinstatement.
It is strenuously argued that the initial termination order dated 20.03.2012 was passed in flagrant violation of the principles of natural justice.
The petitioner, being a permanent employee since 2008, could only be removed in accordance with the Rules.

It is submitted that neither proper charge sheet was issued, nor was a regular departmental inquiry conducted prior to the termination.
6.
Learned counsel emphasizes that the learned Trial Court in S.T. No.73/2015 specifically recorded a finding that the experience certificate was not forged.
It is further submitted that the criminal case was an outcome of malice related to a contempt petition against the Collector.
It is finally urged that the mere pendency of an appeal against acquittal is no ground to deny reinstatement.
The petitioner prays for quashing of the dismissal orders and seeks reinstatement with full back wages, contending that he was not gainfully employed during the intervening period.
7. Per contra, learned counsel for the respondents supports the impugned orders.

It is submitted that the petitioner's representation was considered and rejected by the Respondent No. 3 after due application 5 NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-IND:4156 of mind in compliance with the order passed in W.P. No. 896/2024.
The respondents contend that the dismissal was based on a complaint received from one Pradeep Vyas.

A three-member committee was constituted to conduct an inquiry, which found that the petitioner's brother, the then Block Resources Co-ordinator, had Ashish Sharma vs Collector Shajapur on 5 February, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/188793031/
2 extended undue advantage to the petitioner by issuing fabricated documents.
8.
It is submitted that the inquiry was conducted following the procedure and principles of natural justice, and the charges were found proved.
Consequently, the dismissal order dated 20.03.2012 is justified.
Regarding the acquittal, the respondents submit that the State has preferred Criminal Appeal No. 10847/2023 against the judgment dated 28.03.2023.
Since the appeal is pending before this Hon'ble Court, the petitioner is estopped from claiming reinstatement, and the representation was rightly rejected.

9. Heard both parties at length and examined the entire record available.
10.
It is an undisputed fact that the petitioner was a permanent teacher at the time of his dismissal.

The law is well-settled that a permanent employee carries a right to the post and cannot be dismissed without a strict adherence to the statutory procedure, which invariably includes the issuance of a charge sheet, holding of a regular 6 NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-IND:4156 departmental inquiry, examining witnesses, and affording the delinquent employee a reasonable opportunity to defend himself.

11. The respondents claim that a "three-member committee"
conducted an inquiry.

However, the nature of this inquiry appears to be that of a preliminary fact finding inquiry rather than a disciplinary inquiry under the Madhya Pradesh Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1966.

entities.text: Madhya Pradesh Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1966
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: A preliminary inquiry cannot substitute a regular departmental inquiry where a major penalty like dismissal is imposed.
The petitioner has categorically stated that he was dismissed without giving any proper opportunity of hearing.
The respondents have failed to place on record any evidence demonstrating that a charge sheet was served upon the petitioner or that he was allowed to cross-examine the witnesses.
In the absence of such material, the order dated 20.03.2012 is vitiated by the violation of audi alteram partem.

12. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the recent decision of Sandeep Kumar vs. GB Pant Institute of Engineering & Technology Ghurdauri & Ors., 2024 INSC 309, has held as under:-
"19.

entities.text: Sandeep Kumar vs. GB Pant Institute of Engineering & Technology Ghurdauri & Ors., 2024 INSC 309
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In this background, we are of the firm view that the termination of the services of the appellant without holding disciplinary enquiry was totally unjustified and dehors the requirements of law and in gross violation of principles of 7 NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-IND:4156 natural justice.

Hence, the learned Division Bench of the High Court fell in grave error in dismissing the writ petition filed by the appellant on the hyper technical ground that the minutes of 26th meeting of the Board of Governors dated 16th June, 2018 had not been placed on record."
13.
The primary ground for rejection of the petitioner's request for reinstatement is the pendency of Criminal Appeal No. 10847/2023.
This Court finds this ground legally unsustainable.

The Hon'ble Ashish Sharma vs Collector Shajapur on 5 February, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/188793031/
3

Supreme Court in the case of Capt. M. Paul Anthony v. Bharat Gold Mines Ltd., (1999) 3 SCC 679,
held that where the departmental proceedings and the criminal case are based on the same set of facts and the evidence in both the proceedings is common without there being any variance, the acquittal of the employee in the criminal case should generally lead to his reinstatement.

entities.text: Capt. M. Paul Anthony v. Bharat Gold Mines Ltd., (1999) 3 SCC 679
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
Which reads as under:-
"34.
There is yet another reason for discarding the whole of the case of the respondents.

As pointed out earlier, the criminal case as also the departmental proceedings were based on identical set of facts, namely, "the raid conducted at the appellant's residence and recovery of incriminating articles therefrom".

The findings recorded by the enquiry officer, a copy of which has been placed before us, indicate that the charges framed against the appellant were sought to be proved by police officers and panch witnesses, who had raided the house of the appellant and had effected recovery.

They were the only witnesses examined by the enquiry officer and the enquiry officer, relying upon their statements, came to the conclusion that the charges were established 8 NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-IND:4156 against the appellant.

The same witnesses were examined in the criminal case but the Court, on a consideration of the entire evidence, came to the conclusion that no search was conducted nor was any recovery made from the residence of the appellant.
The whole case of the prosecution was thrown out and the appellant was acquitted.

In this situation, therefore, where the appellant is acquitted by a judicial pronouncement with the finding that the "raid and recovery" at the residence of the appellant were not proved, it would be unjust, unfair and rather oppressive to allow the findings recorded at the ex parte departmental proceedings to stand.

35. Since the facts and the evidence in both the proceedings, namely, the departmental proceedings and the criminal case were the same without there being any iota of difference, the distinction, which is usually drawn as between the departmental proceedings and the criminal case on the basis of approach and burden of proof, would not be applicable to the instant case.

36. For the reasons stated above, the appeal is allowed, the impugned judgment passed by the Division Bench of the High Court is set aside and that of the learned Single Judge, insofar as it purports to allow the writ petition, is upheld.
The learned Single Judge has also given liberty to the respondents to initiate fresh disciplinary proceedings.

In the peculiar circumstances of the case, specially having regard to the fact that the appellant is undergoing this agony since 1985 despite having been acquitted by the criminal court in 1987, we would not direct any fresh departmental enquiry to be instituted against him on the same set of facts.

The appellant shall be reinstated forthwith on the post of Security Officer and shall also be paid the entire arrears of 9 NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-IND:4156 salary, together with all allowances from the date of suspension till his reinstatement, within three months.
The appellant would also be entitled to his cost which is quantified at Rs 15,000."

4 14.
In the instant case, the allegation that forgery of an experience certificate was the subject matter of both the administrative action and the criminal trial.

The learned Trial Court, in its judgment dated 28.03.2023, has not merely acquitted the petitioner on technical grounds but has arrived at a specific finding regarding the genuineness of the document.
The Trial Court opined that "the certificate is not forged."

Once a competent judicial forum has returned a finding of fact that the document is genuine, the administrative authorities cannot cling to a contrary view based on a preliminary committee report to deny the petitioner his livelihood.

The author of the alleged forged document, on the basis of which petitioner was terminated, was examined before the trial court but for the best reasons known to the said authority of respondents, he has not categorically denied the signature before the said authority to be forged.
Even the report of the hand writing expert confirms the signature of the authority who has issued the alleged certificate.
Thus, this Court is of the considered view that on the basis of the findings of the trial court, there is no iota of doubt regarding the genuineness of the certificate in question.

15. Furthermore, regarding the pendency of the appeal, this Court 10 NEUTRAL CITATION NO.
2026:MPHC-IND:4156 holds that mere pendency of an appeal against acquittal does not operate as a stay on the acquittal order.
Unless the appellate court specifically stays the operation of the judgment of acquittal, the employee is entitled to the benefits flowing from such acquittal.

The respondents' refusal to reinstate the petitioner solely on the ground of the pending appeal is,
therefore, arbitrary.
Administrative orders cannot hold a citizen's rights in abeyance indefinitely merely because the State has chosen to file an appeal.

As of today, the petitioner stands acquitted,
and the stigma of forgery stands washed away by the judgment of the Trial Court.
16. The petitioner has prayed for back wages.
The normal rule is "no work, no pay."

However, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Deepali Gundu Surwase v. Kranti Junior Adhyapak Mahavidyalaya,
(2013) 10 SCC 324, has laid down that where the employer's action is found to be illegal, malicious,
or in violation of statutory rules, and where the employee was willing to work but was prevented from doing so, the Court may award back wages.

Deepali Gundu Surwase v. Kranti Junior Adhyapak Mahavidyalaya,
(2013) 10 SCC 324
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In the present case, the termination was illegal as it was passed without a proper inquiry.
Moreover, the petitioner was prevented from discharging his duties due to the unilateral action of the respondents.

However, the petitioner has not placed conclusive proof on record to demonstrate that he remained wholly unemployed during the long intervening period from 2012 to 11 NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-IND:4156 2024.
17.
Balancing the equities, and considering that the burden to prove "non-employment" lies on the employee, this Court deems it appropriate to restrict the back wages.
Since the respondents failed to prove the forgery in the criminal court and failed to conduct a proper inquiry, the petitioner cannot be denied the fruits of his exoneration entirely.
Accordingly, this Court is of the considered view that the petitioner is entitled to 50% of the back wages.
This strikes a balance between the public exchequer's interest and the prejudice caused to the petitioner by an illegal termination.
18. Consequently, the petition deserves to be and is hereby allowed.

The impugned order dated 20.03.2012 (Annexure P/3) passed by the Respondent No. 3 terminating the services of the petitioner and the impugned order dated 17.09.2024 (Annexure P/18) rejecting the petitioner's representation are hereby quashed.

5 19.
The Respondents are directed to reinstate the petitioner in service to his former post of Permanent Teacher forthwith.
The petitioner shall be entitled to notional pay fixation and continuity of service for all purposes, including pension and seniority, as if his services were never terminated.
The petitioner shall be paid 50% of the back wages for the period from the date of termination till the date of reinstatement.
12 NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-IND:4156 20.
The aforesaid exercise shall be completed within a period of 60 days from the date of receipt of a certified copy of this order.
21. Accordingly, the Writ Petition is allowed.
22. Pending applications shall be disposed off accordingly.

(Jai Kumar Pillai) Judge hk/
